goals: Choose between one-sample, two-sample and paired t-tests
Read a t-statistic and its p-value
why: The t-test, invented by William Gosset to monitor Guinness beer quality, is still the workhorse for comparing two means: before vs after, plant A vs plant B.
explain: A **t-test** asks whether a difference in means is large compared with the noise. t = difference ÷ standard error of the difference.

**One-sample**: is this mean different from a target (do bottles contain 500 ml)? **Two-sample (Welch)**: do two independent groups differ? **Paired**: the same units measured twice (before/after training).
Paired tests are far more powerful when they apply, because each unit acts as its own control and removes person-to-person variation.
Assumptions: independent observations and roughly normal data (or reasonably large samples). Use Welch's version by default; it does not assume equal variances.

formula.plain: t = observed difference divided by its standard error (how many "noise units" apart the means are).

example.title: One-sample: is the filling machine on target?
example.result: Reject H₀: the machine underfills by about 2.5 ml and the whole interval lies below 500. Recalibrate; the fix is cheap and underfilling risks regulatory trouble.

mistakes: Using an independent t-test on paired data.
Running t-tests on many pairs of groups (use ANOVA, or correct for multiple comparisons).
takeaways: Welch's t-test as the default for two groups
use: Comparing two means with small to moderate samples

check.q: Same 20 employees tested before and after training. Which test?
